# Workshop 5
 
 # Citizen Assemblies and AI
 
 **Speaker:** Claudia Chwalisz (Founder/CEO, Democracy Next) ( [view bio](https:/www.linkedin.com/in/claudiachwalisz) )
 
 Claudia Chwalisz presents on citizens’ assemblies — randomly selected groups of residents who deliberate on policy questions — and how AI tools can support their quality and spread. The session covers what citizens’ assemblies are, why they matter, and five distinct ways to think about scaling deliberation.
 
 She has worked on democratic innovation for fifteen years, beginning with research on populism and the relationship between political disillusionment and lack of agency in decision-making. [She established and led the OECD’s work on innovative citizen participation from 2018 to 2022, building an evidence base of hundreds of assemblies and developing international standards for their institutionalization.](https:/www.oecd.org/en/publications/innovative-citizen-participation-and-new-democratic-institutions_339306da-en.html)
 
 Chwalisz co-designed the first permanent citizens’ assemblies in Paris, Ostelbelgien, and Brussels, and now leads [Democracy Next](https:/www.demnext.org) , an international research and action institute focused on scaling high-quality, empowered, and permanent citizens’ assemblies with the [MIT Center for Constructive Communication.](https:/www.ccc.mit.edu)
 
 ## What are citizens’assemblies?
 
 Chwalisz frames citizens’ assemblies as a response to two problems: people lack the agency to shape decisions that affect their lives, and existing governance systems struggle with complex, long-term issues. The hypothesis driving her work is that greater agency leads to strong trust, less polarization, and a stronger sense of belonging. Assemblies function as “brave spaces” that leverage collective intelligence to find common ground on difficult questions.
 
 Three principles distinguish citizens’ assemblies from other participation mechanisms:
 
 (1) Sortition: Random selection of participants, producing groups broadly representative of the community. Chwalisz uses the term “sortition” deliberately, noting it is no more technical than “elections,” just less familiar. The practice dates to ancient Athens and persists in jury systems.
 
 (2) Deliberation: Collectively weighing shared evidence with the goal of reaching a decision. Unlike dialogue (coming together to talk), deliberation has a structured process aimed at 75-80% consensus on final recommendations.
 
 (3) Rotation: When assemblies become permanent institutions, rotation ensures new groups of people take on the privilege and responsibility of representing others over time.
 
 Participants receive compensation for their time, childcare, and transport costs to remove barriers to participation. This distinguishes assemblies from volunteer-based engagement and is central to achieving representative samples.
 
 [The OECD documented](https:/www.oecd.org/en/topics/sub-issues/open-government-and-citizen-participation/innovative-public-participation.html) over 700 government-commissioned assemblies globally as of 2023; Chwalisz estimates the current total is closer to 1,000.
 
 Topics cluster around complex issues that are not binary and often have longer-term horizons. The OECD has developed international standards and evaluation guidelines based on this evidence base.
 
 ## 
 
 ## Deschutes County, Oregon
 
 The Deschutes Civic Assembly on Youth Homelessness brought together 30 randomly selected residents over five days (spread across 4-5 weeks) to address the question: “What should be our priorities for building community solutions to prevent and end youth homelessness?” The assembly produced 23 recommendations directed at the Central Oregon Governmental Council, Deschutes County, and the City of Bend. This was also a “tech-enhanced” assembly — a pilot to record all small-group conversations using tools like those described below (see #5).
 
 Chwalisz shared a video clip of one participant describing the experience as “the first time in her life that she has felt her voice mattered.” A one-year follow-up interview documents impacts on policy and moves toward permanent infrastructure in Central Oregon ( [Democracy Next case study](https:/www.demnext.org/projects/deschutes-civic-assembly) ).
 
 ## 
 
 ## Five dimensions of scaling democratic deliberation
 
 Chwalisz and colleague Sammy McKinney developed a framework to clarify conversations about scaling, published as “Five Dimensions of Scaling Democratic Deliberation with and beyond AI” ( [McKinney & Chwalisz 2025](https:/www.demnext.org/projects/five-dimensions-of-scaling-democratic-deliberation-with-and-beyond-ai) ). The dimensions identified in the framework are:
 
 (1) Scaling Out: Increasing the number of people in a single deliberative process. Goals include greater representativeness, legitimacy, and the spread of participation benefits. AI applications include facilitation, support, and sense-making. Chwalisz notes that assumptions often built into this framing include online-only processes, potentially without human facilitators. She raises a critical question: would scaling out actually be cheaper if we maintain standards like participant compensation? "Would this actually be cheaper, or would it be horrendously more expensive if we actually want to fulfill the democratic goals?"
 
 (2) Scaling Up: Deliberation at higher governance levels. Examples include global citizens' assemblies on climate and EU-level panels with participants from 27 countries deliberating in 24 languages. AI translation and interpretation tools show promise but struggle with nuance, accents, satire, and jokes. Multilingual functionality is also relevant at local levels — Chwalisz is involved in an assembly in Luxembourg that will operate in five languages.
 
 (3) Scaling Across: Increasing the number of deliberative processes (assemblies in every county, city, university, museum). AI applications focus on practitioners and organizers: streamlining sortition, automating onboarding, preparing information packages, and creating "assembly assistants." The goal is to enable more people to run high-quality processes with less burden.
 
 (4) Scaling Deep: Increasing impact through institutionalization and connections to the public sphere. This is "probably the one where AI things are the least important" because the work is fundamentally human and relational, involving coalition-building, legal changes, and earning trust. AI can help communicate outputs and support report writing but cannot substitute for the political work of shifting power.
 
 (5) Scaling In: Increasing the quality of deliberation within processes. Chwalisz describes this as the dimension she is "most excited about." Goals include legitimacy, inclusiveness, transparency, and trust. Applications include more inclusive learning materials for different learning styles; sense-making from recorded small group conversations; visualizing conversation dynamics; and identifying absent perspectives (the "empty chair" concept—AI surfacing viewpoints no participant has raised).
 
 ## DelibTech network and tool examples
 
 In October 2024, Democracy Next and the [AI and Democracy Foundation](https:/aidemocracyfoundation.org) launched the [DelibTech Network](https:/www.demnext.org/projects/delibtech-network) , bringing together 40 technologists and deliberative practitioners. The goal is to ensure tools serve real practitioner needs by bridging the two communities. Chwalisz presented three open-source examples from the network.
 
 [MIT Center for Constructive Communication:](http:/ccc.mit.edu) Two tech-enhanced student assemblies were recorded, including small-group deliberations. A tool developed by a master’s student tracks how final recommendations evolved from initial conversations, with links to audio clips. Another student developed “conversation jellies,” visualizations of turn-taking, dominance, and responsivity. An open research question: if participants see this data mid-assembly, does it improve their deliberative behavior?
 
 [Dembrane:](http:/dembrane.com) European open-source tool, GDPR-compliant. Uses QR codes; only one person per table needs a smartphone. Records all small group conversations simultaneously, with a backend interface for practitioners. Supports RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) searches for transcripts and fast synthesis on themes. Tested live with 70 people. Key advantage: sharing synthesized insights back to participants for sense-checking (“does this resonate with what your conversations were?”). Chwalisz says this provides a “fuller, less biased sense” than traditional “popcorning,” where a few people summarize their groups.
 
 [Frankly:](http:/frankly.org) Online-only deliberation platform from the Berkman Klein Center’s Applied Social Media Lab. Features include: large-scale breakout group management; hostless conversations; livestreaming; algorithmic group matching for maximum diversity; embedded discussion prompts; and participation nudges (private messages encouraging quiet participants to speak, or gently flagging over-participation).
 
 ## Takeaways for learners
 
 The five-dimensional framework is the main intellectual contribution here. “Scaling” gets thrown around constantly in this space, but Chwalisz and McKinney break it into distinct goals, like more people (out), higher governance levels (up), more processes (across), deeper institutionalization (deep), better quality (in), each with different implications for where AI helps. This framework is a useful corrective to vague claims about “scaling deliberation.”
 
 What’s also notable is where Chwalisz sees promise and where she doesn’t. She’s skeptical of AI for “scaling deep” as the coalition-building work and trust-earning required to institutionalize assemblies is relational work that can’t be automated. She also pushes back against the assumption that AI-enabled processes are necessarily cheaper: if you’re still paying participants, providing childcare, maintaining accessibility, etc., scaling out might cost more, not less. But she’s excited about “scaling in” — using AI to improve process quality. Recording small group conversations, visualizing turn-taking and dominance, and surfacing unspoken perspectives. That might be the most promising near-term application for these tools.
 
 The tools presented (Dembrane, MIT’s conversation tracking, Frankly) can also map to different dimensions, which is useful for showing the different senses of “AI for deliberation.” And the Deschutes example offers a concrete before/after: 30 people, five days, 23 recommendations, documented policy impact a year later.
 
 It is also worth distinguishing in-depth assemblies from lighter-touch engagements. The structured process (5+ days, consensus-seeking, compensation, sortition) produces outcomes different from those of town halls or comment periods. Think about when each is appropriate.
 
 ## Audience notes
 
 ### Questions
 
 “The challenge of involving people who do not have the time to devote to multi-day assemblies (e.g., low-income workers; those with family duties; people with certain disabilities).”
 
 “How have civic assemblies been funded?”
 
 “Would you let the participants know about the use of AI during the deliberation processes? How and in what ways? What if the participants have misgivings or discomfort about the use of AI, as many of the public do? And is there any way that the participants and organizers co-design AI use in deliberative processes, as doing so would increase the legitimacy of the processes?"
 
 ### Participant locations and affiliations
 
 Arizona, Tennessee, Syria, Hungary, Massachusetts (Amherst), Washington DC (governance specialist), California (Better Together America/Thriving Together US/NCDD network), Dublin (longtime Democracy Next follower), New Jersey, and others. The audience included practitioners from collective impact networks, EU communication professionals, and democracy/governance specialists.
 
 ## Quotes
 
 ### Claudia Chwalisz (Democracy Next)
 
 "Around the world, people lack agency to shape the decisions that affect their lives."
 
 "Our governance systems, as they have been designed and kind of implemented for quite a long time, are in some ways failing to address the hard, most complex issues that are kind of exemplary of our time today."
 
 "Citizens' assemblies are brave spaces which allow for us to be able to leverage our collective intelligence, to be with the complexity of the issues that we face, and to find common ground with one another."
 
 "Sortition might sound like a wonky or unfamiliar word, but I'm using it intentionally because I think it's just unfamiliar, and there's nothing more wonky about it than elections."
 
 "People get paid to be part of these assembly processes. They get paid for their time, and childcare is provided, and transport costs are covered, that we break down the barriers to participation and make this possible for anyone to be part of it."
 
 On scaling out: "Would this actually be cheaper, or would it be horrendously more expensive if we actually want to fulfill the democratic goals of paying people and making it possible for everyone to participate equally?"
 
 On AI translation: "The tools are not very good yet at capturing things around nuance, accents, satire, and jokes."
 
 On scaling deep: "This is probably the one where AI things are the least important... that's very human relational work that actually starts to shift power."
 
 On Dembrane: "There's no claim that this is going to be perfect, but it is fast... I think this gives a better, deeper sense of what happened... this is more insightful than popcorning, like, 5 people to share what they talked about in their small group conversation."
 
 "The path towards scaled deliberation is about bridging technological innovation with democracy's fundamental human elements... trust, the connection, the understanding, the collective agency."
 
 ## 
 
 ## Resources
 
 [Democracy Next](https:/demnext.org) — International research and action institute focused on scaling permanent citizens' assemblies. Led by Claudia Chwalisz.
 
 [OECD Innovative Citizen Participation](https:/www.oecd.org/governance/innovative-citizen-participation) — Evidence base of 700+ assemblies, international standards, and evaluation guidelines. Built during Chwalisz's tenure at OECD (2018–2022).
 
 [MIT Center for Constructive Communication](https:/ccc.mit.edu) — Tech-enhanced assembly research. Collaboration with Democracy Next on pop-up lab. Tools for tracking idea evolution and visualizing conversation dynamics.
 
 [Dembrane](https:/www.dembrane.com) — European open-source tool for recording and analyzing small group conversations. GDPR compliant. Uses QR codes so only one person per table needs a smartphone. RAG search of transcripts.
 
 [Frankly](https:/www.frankly.org) — Online deliberation platform from Berkman Klein Center's Applied Social Media Lab. Features algorithmic group matching, participation nudges, hostless conversations, and livestreaming.
 
 [DelibTech Network](https:/www.demnext.org/projects/delibtech-network) — Launched October 2024 by Democracy Next and AI and Democracy Foundation. 40 technologists and deliberative practitioners. Goal to ensure tools serve practitioner needs.
 
 [McKinney & Chwalisz (2025) "Five Dimensions of Scaling Democratic Deliberation with and beyond AI"](https:/www.demnext.org/projects/five-dimensions-of-scaling-democratic-deliberation-with-and-beyond-ai) — Paper providing the five-dimension framework discussed in the presentation.
